exploration.title: Moon Phase Observatory
exploration.subject: Space science
exploration.summary: Change the Moon’s orbital position and compare the sunlit fraction seen from Earth with the Sun–Earth–Moon geometry.
exploration.question: How does the Moon’s position around Earth change the phase we see?
exploration.explanation: The Sun illuminates half the Moon. As the Moon travels around Earth, our viewpoint reveals changing portions of that sunlit hemisphere. The mean phase cycle from new Moon to new Moon is about 29.53 days, not the 27.32-day sidereal orbit relative to the stars. The model uses a circular, coplanar orbit with enlarged objects and gaps; it does not predict local sky orientation, libration, eclipses, terrain shadows, or exact timing.

experiments.title: Test first quarter
experiments.instruction: Predict 25%, 50%, or 75% illuminated at 90°. Keep the Sun direction and Earth viewpoint fixed, then observe first quarter.
experiments.observe: Half of the visible disk is lit at 90°. Explain the distinction between half the visible disk and half the whole Moon always receiving sunlight.

experiments.title: Compare opposite quarters
experiments.instruction: Predict whether first quarter at 90° or last quarter at 270° has a larger visible lit fraction. Compare them from the same Earth viewpoint.
experiments.observe: Both are 50% lit, on opposite sides. Explain why equal fractions can have different phase names without Earth casting a shadow.

exploration.misconception: The usual Moon phases are not Earth’s shadow. Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse, a separate event that does not happen every month.
